## Intro

Somewhere in Florida, the price on a house has been cut nine times, and today it's listed $170,000 below where it started. Another house was bought in 2013 for $70,100, and it's now for sale at more than three and a half times that. A third went under contract with a buyer this summer, and the very next day it was back on the market.

So why are some Florida homes selling while others just sit and wait?

Here's what this spring showed. Of the counties we checked, the ones where prices have dropped well below their peak almost all sold more homes this spring than last spring. The ones where prices are still near the top split about evenly, with some gaining buyers and some losing them. Those two pictures sit side by side, and this video walks through both.

Welcome to The Housing Atlas. We're counting down ten Florida counties, with real houses, real prices, and real numbers, and number one isn't where you'd expect.

Let's get into it.

## 10 · Lee County

We start the countdown at number ten, Lee County, with one house in Fort Myers whose price has been cut nine times. The owner bought it in 2017 for $310,000 and put it on the market in August 2024 at $580,000. Today, a little over two years later, it's listed at $410,000. That's $170,000 lower, the biggest drop of any house in this countdown.

Across Lee County, prices have come down as well. This spring, homes here sold for about 13 percent less than at their peak in the summer of 2022, and no county on this list has fallen further from its peak. Prices were a little lower than last spring, too. Even so, about 10 percent more homes sold this spring than the spring before.

That's one side of the picture this video is about, and nowhere on this list is it plainer than here.

This is Florida's southwest coast, where roughly three in every ten people are over 65. Prices here peaked in June 2022. Three months later, on September 28th, Hurricane Ian hit Cayo Costa as a Category 4 storm. The National Hurricane Center says 41 people in the United States died in its storm surge, and 36 of them were in Lee County, where more than 5,000 structures were destroyed.

Arthur Jones, a minister at a Unitarian Universalist congregation in Fort Myers, told NPR last November that people were moving away "because they're tired of having to rebuild. They're tired of the high costs. They're tired of the anxiety that comes from hurricane season."

So for anyone who owns a home here, homes are selling for clearly less than they did in 2022, and for anyone thinking of buying, this is a market below its peak, in a spring when more people bought than the year before.

Now we leave the coast for The Villages, in Sumter County, at number nine.

## 9 · Sumter County

Number nine is Sumter County, home of The Villages, and the best way into it is something Joel Berner, a senior economist at Realtor.com, told Villages-News.com in September: "Prices in The Villages have been softening since 2022 as the pace of sales has slowed and the inventory of homes has grown." It's a gentle word, and it fits.

Nothing sudden happened here; the change came slowly, as the number of homes for sale kept climbing. In May 2025, there were 764 homes for sale in the county, the most in any month since July 2016. By August of this year, there were fewer than a year earlier, but still about 80 percent more than in August 2019.

Prices, meanwhile, have barely moved. The peak came in September 2022, and this spring prices were only about three and a half percent under it. So a home here sells for about what it did a year ago, a little below where prices peaked. Slightly fewer homes sold, about 3 percent fewer than the spring before. It's a quiet market.

More than half of the people in Sumter County are over 65, the highest share of any county in Florida. Not long ago, this was also the fastest-growing metro in the country: the Census Bureau gave the Wildwood–The Villages area that ranking for 2022 to 2023.

Back in August 2024, someone paid $424,000 for a house here, and eleven months later, in July 2025, it went up for sale at $460,000. After four price cuts, it's listed at $399,900, about $24,000 below what the owner paid two years ago, and it has been on the market for about fourteen months.

Next, we head to the northwest of the state, to number eight, Bay County.

## Mid-video hook

That's five down. So far, we've seen places where prices came down and more people bought, places where prices held near the top, and Polk, where prices slipped a little and fewer people bought anyway. Still ahead are a town that lost its hospital, a house that was under contract for a single day, a county where nearly half the sellers cut their prices and homes still sold at the top, and a number one that might surprise you. If this is helping you make sense of Florida's housing market, take a second to subscribe. Now, let's keep going.

## 1 · Highlands County

Number one on our countdown is Highlands County, home to Sebring, Avon Park, and Lake Placid, and it isn't on the coast at all. This is an inland retirement area where more than a third of the people are over 65, and homes are typically worth about half as much as across Florida.

Ian reached this county as flooding that held up getting the power back on and checking the damage. Gloria Rybinski, a spokesperson for Highlands County, said at the time: "For some people, it's more dramatic to see your roof gone. But it's just as hard to see your living room flooded."

In Sebring, a seller even pushed the asking price on a house back up once, by $1,000, in October 2025, a week after its second cut. It went on the market in July 2025 at $275,000 and, after four cuts in all, it's listed at $255,000, about fifteen months later. The owner bought it in 2013 for $70,100, and today's asking price is more than three and a half times that.

Prices here haven't come down at all: this spring they matched their peak, and they were about 4 percent higher than a year earlier. But about 18 percent fewer homes sold this spring than the spring before, the biggest drop in this countdown, and sales had fallen the spring before that, too.

We began this countdown in Fort Myers, where prices had fallen further than anywhere else on the list and more people were buying. Highlands sits at the other end. Between those two ends is the pattern of this whole spring: where prices had dropped well below their peak, sales rose in all but two of the counties we checked, and where prices held near the top, it went both ways. Citrus, at number four, held at the top and gained buyers. Highlands held at the top and lost more of them than anywhere else on this list.

So if you own a home here, what homes sell for hasn't come down from the top, but this spring clearly fewer people bought than two years ago, and the number of homes for sale is growing.

Now let's step back and see what the whole countdown adds up to.

## Closing

That's our countdown: ten counties, ten houses, and a spring that looked very different depending on where you were.

Where prices have come down from their peak, as they have around Fort Myers, Punta Gorda, and Naples, more people bought homes this spring. Where prices have held near the top, the answer was mixed, with some places, like Crystal River, drawing more buyers, and others, like Sebring, seeing far fewer. That doesn't prove one thing causes the other, but it's how this spring played out.

So here's a prediction you can hold us to. The numbers for this summer, June through August, aren't in yet. When they are, we expect that in at least two out of three of the counties we checked where prices sit at least 5 percent below their peak, more homes will have sold this summer than last summer. This spring, it was 11 out of 13. We'll check in January 2027 and tell you whether we got it right. If we didn't, then what we saw this spring belonged to this spring alone.

If you live in Florida, or you're thinking about moving there, tell us in the comments what you're seeing where you are. Are homes selling, or are they sitting?

If you'd like to be here when we check that prediction, subscribe to The Housing Atlas.

This video is for information only and isn't financial or real estate advice. Sales and price figures come from Redfin and run through May 2026. Figures on homes for sale and price cuts come from FRED and run through August 2026, and the asking prices on the houses come from their listings in early October 2026.
